Fractional-N: uses sigma-delta modulation of the divider to achieve fractional division ratios, giving fine frequency resolution without reducing the reference frequency. Quantization noise from the modulator must be filtered by the loop.

For microwave and optical frequencies: use frequency multiplication (each doubling adds 6 dB of phase noise), offset mixing (translate from a synthesized IF to the microwave output), or an optical frequency comb (mode-locked laser producing equally spaced frequency lines spanning an octave, referenced to an atomic clock via f-2f self-referencing).

Compute the output phase noise. Within the PLL bandwidth: L_out(f) = L_ref(f) + 20*log10(N) + L_PD(f) + L_CP(f) where the last two terms are phase detector and charge pump noise contributions. Outside the PLL bandwidth: L_out(f) = L_VCO(f). The total phase noise is the combination. For DDS: L_out(f) = L_clock(f) + quantization noise floor + DAC noise floor.

Compute the spurious performance. PLL spurs: reference spurs at multiples of the reference frequency, level depends on charge pump leakage and loop filter rejection. Fractional-N spurs: from the sigma-delta modulator, at offsets related to the fractional ratio. DDS spurs: from phase truncation and DAC nonlinearity, can be predicted from the frequency tuning word.

Document the synthesizer design with a block diagram, component selection (PLL IC, VCO, DDS chip, loop filter values), simulated phase noise plot, spurious map, lock time, and frequency switching speed. Compare the achieved performance against the requirements.

steps.description: Design a system to distribute precise time and frequency from a reference to remote locations using GNSS, fiber, or network-based methods.

inputs.name: synthesizer-design
inputs.desc: Local frequency synthesis system

inputs.name: distribution-requirements
inputs.desc: Required time accuracy at remote sites, distance, available infrastructure

outputs.name: time-distribution-design
outputs.desc: Selected distribution method with accuracy analysis and equipment specification

outputs.name: achieved-accuracy
outputs.desc: Expected time and frequency accuracy at each remote site

process: Select the distribution method by accuracy and infrastructure. GPS common-view: compare two GPS receivers at different sites, subtract the common satellite errors. Accuracy: 2-10 ns over intercontinental baselines. Requires GPS receiver and antenna at each site. Two-way satellite time transfer (TWSTT): exchange timing signals through a geostationary satellite, cancel the path delay by symmetry. Accuracy: 0.5-2 ns. Requires satellite modem and antenna.

For local distribution (within a facility): coaxial cable or fiber distribution of 1PPS and 10 MHz reference. Cable delay: ~5 ns/m for coax, ~5 ns/m for fiber. Compensate with measured delay. For high accuracy: round-trip measurement of cable delay and automatic correction. Temperature coefficient of cable delay: ~100 ppm/C for standard coax. Phase-stabilized fiber links achieve sub-picosecond stability over 100+ km.

IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol (PTP) for network-based distribution. PTP uses timestamped packets exchanged between master and slave clocks to measure and compensate network delay. Hardware timestamping at the PHY layer reduces jitter. Accuracy: 10-100 ns on a well-designed LAN with PTP-aware switches (boundary clocks or transparent clocks). Accuracy degrades across routers and non-PTP switches.

White Rabbit: an extension of PTP using syntonization (frequency locking via the Ethernet physical layer) and precise phase measurement. Achieves sub-nanosecond accuracy over fiber links of 10+ km. Used in CERN, financial trading, and telecom.

Design the monitoring and verification system. Each remote site needs a method to verify that it is receiving correct time. Cross-check between distribution methods where possible (e.g., GPS vs PTP). Monitor the time offset at each site and alarm on exceedance. For critical applications, maintain a local holdover clock that continues to provide time during distribution outages.

Document the distribution architecture, the equipment at each site, the expected accuracy under normal and degraded conditions (e.g., GPS jamming, network congestion, fiber cut), and the monitoring and alarm system.
